clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant ataxia dominated by a severe large-fibre sensory axonal neuropathy, so proprioceptive loss and areflexia are as prominent as the cerebellar signs.
Gastrointestinal symptoms — recurrent vomiting and abdominal pain — were a striking feature in the originally described French family, an unusual accompaniment among the spinocerebellar ataxias.
There is a wide range of onset, from childhood to adult life, with marked variability even within families.
Mapped to the short arm of chromosome 2 (around 2p21-p15); variants in PNPT1 have recently been implicated as causative.
Nerve conduction studies show a sensory neuronopathy or ganglionopathy with reduced or absent sensory potentials.
Core cerebellar features include gait ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus.
It is distinguished from SCA4 (ZFHX3, 16q22) and SCA18 by its locus and gene and, in some families, by the gastrointestinal involvement.
reference.pathophysiology: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 25 is an autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia mapped to the short arm of chromosome 2 (around 2p21-p15), in which variants in PNPT1 — encoding polyribonucleotide nucleotidyltransferase 1, a mitochondrial RNA-processing and import enzyme — have recently been identified as causative. Impaired mitochondrial RNA handling is thought to drive degeneration of dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons, producing a prominent sensory neuronopathy, together with cerebellar pathways and, in some families, gastrointestinal dysfunction. The resulting phenotype pairs a severe large-fibre sensory neuropathy with progressive cerebellar ataxia, contrasting with the sensorimotor pattern of SCA18 and overlapping clinically with the sensory-predominant SCA4.
additionalDifferentials: SCA4 (ZFHX3, 16q22) — dominant ataxia with prominent sensory neuropathy
SCA18 (sensorimotor neuropathy with ataxia) — added motor weakness and atrophy
Friedreich ataxia (recessive sensory neuropathy with areflexia and cardiomyopathy)
CANVAS — cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (RFC1)
Acquired sensory neuronopathy (paraneoplastic anti-Hu, Sjogren-related ganglionopathy, vitamin B6 toxicity)
Other dominant cerebellar ataxias associated with peripheral neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of PNPT1 or linkage to the 2p locus where available
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography demonstrating a sensory neuronopathy
MRI brain to assess cerebellar atrophy
Hereditary ataxia gene panel to exclude sibling subtypes
Investigations to exclude acquired sensory neuronopathy (paraneoplastic antibodies, Sjogren screen, vitamin B12 and B6 status)
Gastrointestinal evaluation when vomiting or abdominal symptoms are present
Family pedigree analysis with genetic counselling
redFlags: Subacute sensory neuronopathy raising the possibility of a paraneoplastic cause.
Severe gastrointestinal symptoms with weight loss or dehydration.
Rapid neurological progression atypical for a hereditary ataxia.
Frequent falls resulting from profound proprioceptive loss.
reference.prognosis: Course is variable but generally slowly progressive, with disability arising chiefly from sensory ataxia; lifespan is usually preserved.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing an acquired sensory neuronopathy as this hereditary disorder, or vice versa.
Overlooking gastrointestinal symptoms as a diagnostic clue in affected families.
Assuming a standard repeat-expansion panel will detect the causative variant.
Failing to distinguish it from the sensory-predominant SCA4 without molecular confirmation.
references: Neurogenetics reference texts on autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxias
Standard neurology textbook chapters on inherited ataxias
Consensus reviews of hereditary ataxias with sensory neuronopathy
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, so centre care on sensory-ataxia rehabilitation with proprioceptive retraining, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy
Control neuropathic pain from the severe large-fibre sensory neuronopathy with a gabapentinoid or tricyclic antidepressant
Institute falls prevention with walking aids and home hazard assessment given profound proprioceptive loss and areflexia
Manage the gastrointestinal features with antiemetics for recurrent vomiting, dietetic support and gastroenterology evaluation for the abdominal symptoms
Exclude treatable acquired sensory neuronopathy mimics (paraneoplastic, Sjogren syndrome, and vitamin B12 or B6 disturbance)
Provide multidisciplinary follow-up across neurology, gastroenterology and allied health
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing for the autosomal dominant inheritance
